why: Even 25 mg strongly blocks histamine H1 receptors, so it makes people drowsy within about an hour and helps them fall and stay asleep.
source: Cohrs S et al. (2004) Psychopharmacology 174:421-429, sleep-promoting properties of quetiapine 25 and 100 mg in healthy subjects; Karsten J et al. (2017) J Psychopharmacol 31:327-337

why: Some people feel groggy the morning after a low bedtime dose, though studies of residual next-day effects at 25-50 mg are small and inconsistent.
source: Karsten J et al. (2017) J Psychopharmacol 31:327-337; Seroquel SmPC (somnolence, warning on driving); Anderson SL & Vande Griend JP (2014) Am J Health Syst Pharm 71:394-402 (review of low-dose quetiapine for insomnia)

why: Immediate-release quetiapine peaks in blood about 1-2 hours after a dose and has a half-life of about 7 hours, so drowsiness comes on within the first hour and fades over the rest of the day.
source: DeVane CL & Nemeroff CB (2001) Clin Pharmacokinet 40:509-522 (quetiapine pharmacokinetics: Tmax ~1.5 h, t1/2 ~6-7 h); Seroquel SmPC

why: At 300 mg quetiapine adds strong alpha-1 and further H1 blockade on top of the 25 mg effect, which is why new users are started low and titrated up to avoid heavy sedation and dizziness.
source: Seroquel SmPC / US prescribing information (titration schedule; somnolence dose-related); Cohrs S et al. (2004) Psychopharmacology 174:421-429 (100 mg more sedating than 25 mg on some measures)

why: A 300 mg dose in someone not used to it is markedly sedating; alertness drops sharply for several hours.
source: Seroquel SmPC (somnolence very common, effects on driving/machinery); Leucht S et al. (2013) Lancet 382:951-962 (quetiapine among the more sedating antipsychotics)

why: The heavy sedation at 300 mg slows reaction times and impairs sustained attention in people who do not need the drug.
source: Seroquel SmPC (warning: may impair judgement, thinking or motor skills); Leucht S et al. (2013) Lancet 382:951-962

why: Regular quetiapine (via H1 and 5-HT2C blockade) increases appetite, and people on it gain weight on average over weeks to months.
source: Pillinger T et al. (2020) Lancet Psychiatry 7:64-77 (metabolic effects of antipsychotics meta-analysis); Huhn M et al. (2019) Lancet 394:939-951

why: Over several weeks, 300 mg/day lifts mood more than placebo in bipolar depression and helps as an add-on in major depression, though the extra benefit is modest.
source: Calabrese JR et al. (2005) Am J Psychiatry 162:1351-1360 (BOLDER I); Thase ME et al. (2006) J Clin Psychopharmacol 26:600-609 (BOLDER II); Bauer M et al. (2009) J Clin Psychiatry 70:540-549 (adjunctive XR in MDD)

why: In generalised anxiety disorder trials, about 150 mg/day quetiapine XR lowered anxiety more than placebo, similar to standard antidepressants, but side effects limit its use.
source: Bandelow B et al. (2010) Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 13:305-320; Merideth C et al. (2012) Int Clin Psychopharmacol 27:40-54; Stein DJ et al. (2011) Hum Psychopharmacol (pooled analysis of three 8-week trials, quetiapine XR 50/150/300 mg)

why: Haloperidol barely touches histamine receptors, so a low 2 mg dose is far less sedating than 300 mg quetiapine, which blocks them strongly.
source: Leucht S et al. (2013) Lancet 382:951-962 (sedation by antipsychotic); Kroeze WK et al. (2003) Neuropsychopharmacology 28:519-526 (H1 affinity of antipsychotics)
